title: IMPOSSIBLE PLACES | The Most Incredible Megaprojects on Earth Even Their Builders Can't Explain
fullText: Human beings are very good at building things. We are considerably worse at predicting what happens next. Every project on this list was drawn up by people who were the best in the world at what they did. Engineers with degrees, models, surveys, decades of experience. And every single one of them ended up standing in front of something they had made, holding a report that did not add up. An airport built on an artificial island that started sinking faster than anyone predicted and has never stopped. A tunnel where the mountain itself squeezes inward and slowly crushes the walls. A hole drilled deeper than any hole in history, abandoned because the rock at the bottom began doing something the physics said it should not do. and a chamber being carved into finished bedrock right now designed to keep something dangerous sealed away for a 100,000 years by people who cannot work out how to leave a warning that anybody in a 100,000 years would understand. These are the 15 biggest mega projects on Earth that even their [music] builders cannot fully explain. Before we begin, do me a favor. Drop a comment telling us where you are watching from [music] and what time it is right now. We want to see how far this one travels tonight. Let's start. Number 15. The tallest empty building in the world. Look at a photograph of the Pyongyang skyline in North Korea. And one shape dominates [music] everything. A pyramid 105 stories tall, rising over 300 m with three wings sloping up to a single point. [music] It is called the Ryugong Hotel. Construction began in 1987. As of today, it has never opened. The ambition was enormous. North Korea wanted a hotel that would outscale anything its rivals [music] had built, and the design called for thousands of rooms and revolving restaurants at the top. Concrete went up fast through the late8s. Then the Soviet Union collapsed and with it the economic support North Korea had depended on. Work stopped around 1992 and the building stood as a bare concrete shell for something like 16 years. No windows, no fittings. A crane left rusting on [music] the summit, visible from across the city. There were persistent reports during that period questioning the quality of the concrete and the alignment of the structure and whether it could ever be safely finished at all. Those reports came from outside because independent engineers were not exactly being invited in for a look. In 2008, an Egyptian company clad the exterior in glass, which transformed it. From the outside, it now looks like a finished building. There have been partial openings announced, lighting displays projected across the facade, and periodic reports that a section might open. The interior, by essentially every account that has come out, remains largely unfinished, which produces something genuinely strange. The tallest unoccupied building on the planet in the middle of a capital city, lit up at night, looking complete from every angle a photograph can be taken from. Nobody outside the country can tell you with confidence what is actually inside it. That is a building nobody can get into. Our next project is one that will not stay where its builders put it. [music] Number 14, the airport that will not stop sinking. By the late 1980s, Osaka in Japan had a serious problem. It needed a new international airport and there was no land available. The region is densely built and the old airport was hemmed in by a city that did not want to be woken up at night. So the solution was to build the land. Concai International Airport sits on an artificial island in Osaka Bay around 5 km offshore. Construction began in 1987. Crews leveled hilltops on the mainland and moved an enormous volume of fill out into the bay. They drove hundreds of thousands of vertical sand drains into the seabed to squeeze water out of the soft clay beneath, trying to force decades of natural settlement to happen in advance. The people doing [music] this were not amateurs. They knew the island would sink. That was expected. That was in the plan. It sank faster than the plan. By the time the airport opened in 1994, [music] the island had already settled substantially more than the projections allowed for. Buildings were fitted with adjustable columns, jacks, that let engineers lift sections of the terminal as [music] the ground beneath dropped unevenly. That system is still in use. The airport is in a real sense being manually held up. The settlement has slowed enormously as everyone [music] expected it would. But it has not stopped. And here is what makes it genuinely [music] difficult. The clay layers under Osaka Bay are not uniform. They compress at different rates in different places. And the deeper layers behave in ways that are hard to model precisely. Predictions of how much further it will settle have been repeatedly revised as the real measurements come in. In 2018, a typhoon pushed a storm surge over the island and flooded the runway and terminal, stranding thousands of people. Seaw walls have been raised since. So there it is. One of the busiest airports in Asia on ground that did not exist 40 years ago. Sitting on soft clay in a typhoon zone kept level by hand indefinitely. From an island that keeps dropping to a tunnel that took two centuries of arguing before anyone dug it properly. Number 13. The tunnel under the sea that took 200 years to start. The idea of a tunnel under the English Channel is not modern. A French engineer proposed one seriously in 1802, [music] complete with ventilation chimneys rising out of the water and a halfway island where horses could be changed. Napoleon reportedly showed interest. It went nowhere. Attempts kept coming through the 19th century. In the 1880s, exploratory tunnels were actually dug from both coasts. Real machinery, real [music] progress over a kilometer driven under the seabed. Then British military anxiety killed it. The argument was simple. A tunnel is a hole in a moat. And Britain's entire defensive logic rested on being an island. Work stopped. Another attempt in the 1970s was cancelled after digging had already begun. The tunnel that finally worked started in 1988 and opened in 1994. Three bores [music] around 50 km with roughly 38 km of that under the seabed. One of the longest undersea tunnel sections in the world. Geology made it possible. A layer of chalk marl runs under the channel relatively soft and relatively watertight and the tunnel follows it. Machines worked from both coasts and the breakthrough came in 1990. The engineering worked, the arithmetic did not. The project ran dramatically over budget and the private consortium financing it went through severe restructuring. shareholders lost enormous sums. It became a textbook case in how badly large infrastructure projects misjudge cost and revenue. Studied by economists ever since, precisely because so many smart people got the numbers so wrong. 200 years of proposals, a tunnel that works beautifully, [music] carries millions of people, and costs so much more than anyone forecast that the people who paid for it never got their money back. That project misjudged money. Our next one changed something considerably larger. Number 12, the dam that moved the day. On the Yangze River in China stands the Three Gorges Dam, the largest power station on the planet by [music] installed capacity. The wall is over 2 km wide and around 180 m high with a reservoir stretching hundreds of kilome upstream. The human cost was written into the plan from the start. Well over a million people were relocated. Entire cities were demolished and rebuilt on higher ground. Temples, towns, and archaeological sites that had stood for centuries went under the water permanently. The project was debated inside China for decades. It was approved by the National People's Congress in 1992 with an unusually large number of abstensions and votes against which in that body is a signal. Then there is the detail that circulates endlessly online. And unusually for these things, there is real science behind it. The reservoir holds an enormous mass of water, and filling it raised that mass higher above sea level than it had been. Moving mass away from the axis of a spinning object changes how it spins. NASA scientists calculated the effect, and the figure that came out was an increase in the length of the day of a fraction of a microscond. a tiny number, also a real one. Human beings built something big enough that the planet's rotation had to be recalculated. The harder questions are still being argued. Reservoir induced seismicity is a genuine field of study, and researchers have looked closely at whether the enormous water load and changing pressure in the rock have influenced seismic activity in the region. Landslides along the reservoir banks have been an ongoing documented problem as levels rise and fall. Sediment that used to travel down the Yangze now settles behind the dam instead with consequences downstream [music] that are still being measured. It generates a staggering amount of clean electricity. It also rearranged a river system that had behaved a certain way for millions of years and that accounting is not finished. That project delivered what it [music] promised at a cost people still argue over. Our next one delivered nothing at all for 9 years. Number 11, the airport that could not be switched on. Berlin decided in the 1990s to consolidate its airports into one modern hub. Construction on Berlin Brandenburgg airport began in 2006. The opening was [music] set for 2011. It opened in 2020. The delay became a national embarrassment. Opening dates were announced and cancelled repeatedly, sometimes within weeks of the date. Invitations went out. Airlines rescheduled operations. Then it was called off again. The core problem was the fire safety system. The smoke extraction design was extraordinarily [music] complex. And when inspectors examined it, it failed, not in a small way. Investigations reportedly identified tens of thousands of defects across the building with cable routing, [music] sprinkler installation, and the fire alarm system all implicated. [music] For years, staff ran lights and systems in the empty terminal simply to stop the equipment degrading, and trains ran through the unused station beneath it to keep the tunnel ventilated. Costs multiplied several times over the original budget. Executives resigned. Parliamentary committees investigated and the airport sat there finished on the outside completely unusable. Now I can hear the objection already. A delayed airport is a management failure, not a mystery. Nobody in Berlin is standing there unable to explain the physics. Fair enough. But Germany has one of the most respected engineering cultures on Earth. This project had money, expertise, oversight, [music] and enormous public attention. And a group of extremely competent people still could not get a building to pass its own fire [music] inspection for the better part of a decade. If that can happen there, the question is not why Berlin failed. [music] It is why we assume anywhere else would do better. Tell me in the comments whether you think this one earns its place. I suspect this is where we split from a project that could not open to a project that is quietly coming apart in the sea. Number 10, the islands that are going backwards. Off the coast of Dubai, the Palm Jira is one of the most recognizable shapes on Earth from the air. A palm tree made of sand with a trunk, 16 fronds, and a curving breakwater around the outside. It was dredged out of the seabed. Enormous volumes of sand were pumped into position and the breakwater [music] built from millions of tons of rock. To compact the fill and reduce the risk of it liquefying in a seismic event, contractors used viro compaction, driving probes into the sand and [music] shaking it into a denser state. It worked. People live there. Its bigger sibling did not fare as well. Nearby, a second project [music] called the world was built. Around 300 artificial islands arranged into a rough map of the continents sold to buyers who wanted their own country in miniature. Then the financial crisis arrived in 2008. Development largely [music] stalled and the sea kept working. Reports emerged that the islands were eroding, that sand was migrating, that channels between them were silting up, and the shapes [music] were losing definition. Those reports were disputed by the developer, and there has been ongoing development on some islands since. But for years, satellite images of the world showed a map of the continents slowly going soft at the edges. And there is a wider problem. Artificial islands change how water moves. Currents that ran along a coastline get interrupted. Sediment accumulates where it is not wanted, and beaches elsewhere lose the sand supply they depended on. Coastal engineers have raised concerns about circulation and water quality behind structures like these [music] because water that does not move well does not stay clean. You can build a map of the world out of sand and make it hold together with rock and money. What you cannot do is tell the ocean to stop rearranging it. From islands the sea keeps editing to a project that went underground and could not find the bottom of its own budget. Number nine, the most expensive road in American history. Boston had an elevated highway running straight through the middle of it. Opened in the 1950s, it carried far more traffic than it was designed for. It was permanently congested, [music] and it cut the city off from its own waterfront with a wall of concrete and steel. The solution was simple to describe and appalling to execute. Take the highway down, put it underground, do it without stopping traffic. The project, officially called the central artery and tunnel [music] project and universally called the Big Dig, ran from 1991 to 2007. [music] Crews had to tunnel underneath a city that was already there, threading around subway lines, utilities, and building foundations while keeping the elevated highway open above their heads. In one section, engineers used ground freezing, driving pipes into the earth and circulating coolant to turn saturated soil into a solid block. so tunneling could proceed beneath active railway lines. It worked. The highway came down, the tunnels went in, and the city got its waterfront back. The cost is what everybody remembers. [music] Original estimates were a fraction of the final figure. With financing included, the total ran well past $14 billion, the most expensive highway project in American history. Then in 2006, ceiling panels in one of the tunnels collapsed onto a car, killing a passenger. The investigation focused on the epoxy anchor system holding the panels, and the resulting inquiry dominated coverage of the project for years. A genuine engineering achievement that people drive through every day without thinking about it, tied permanently to a cost overrun taught in business schools, and to a death that should not have happened. Now, before we get to the top eight, do me one small favor. Hit the like button. It genuinely tells the algorithm to push this to more people who love this kind of thing, and it costs you nothing because the next ones stop being about money and start being about physics that does not cooperate. Number eight, the tunnel where the mountain closes in. Under the Swiss Alps runs the Godard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016. At around 57 kilometers, it is the longest railway tunnel in the world. And at its deepest, it lies roughly 2,300 meters below the mountains above. Building it took 17 years. Two enormous boring machines, plus sections excavated by blasting where the machines could not cope. The reason it took 17 years is that the Alps are not one thing. Boring through a mountain range means passing through a sequence of completely different rock types [music] and each one has its own opinion about being drilled. Some of it was hard, stable granite, which is comparatively good news, [music] and some of it was not. There are zones in these mountains where the rock behaves almost like something thick and slow rather than something solid. Under enormous pressure, certain rock types deform over time. Engineers call it squeezing ground. Once you cut a hole through it, the rock does not sit there. It creeps inward, closing the space you just made, pressing against whatever you installed to hold it open. Tunnel builders in the Alps have dealt with this for well over a century. And [music] the historic Godhard tunnel of the 1870s met exactly this problem. The techniques that work involve giving the rock somewhere to go rather than trying to stop it dead. Yielding supports, deformable elements that compress in a controlled way. linings designed on the assumption that the mountain will push and must be allowed to. Predicting exactly where those zones appear and how badly they behave is extremely difficult even with extensive survey work because you cannot see through 2 km of rock. Crews find out when they get there. Meanwhile, at that depth, rock temperatures climb high enough that the working environment has to be actively cooled for people to function. So, there is a train running under the Alps right now at high speed through a tunnel that took nearly two decades in a mountain that is still very slowly trying to close it. That project fought a mountain that was already there. Our next one proposes to build a mountain of its own. Number seven, the line in the desert. In 2021, Saudi Arabia announced [music] a project called the line, part of the wider neon development. The concept as presented was a city built as a single continuous structure. Two parallel mirrored walls around 500 m tall, stretching 170 km across the desert, roughly 200 m apart. No cars, everything you need within a 5-minute walk. Millions of residents. The renderings were spectacular and went everywhere. Engineers and urban planners raised questions immediately, and they were not unreasonable ones. A linear city means the two ends are 170 km apart, and the proposal relied on high-speed rail beneath it. Mirrored glass at that scale raises serious questions about bird strikes and about heat. A single continuous structure has to be built through varied terrain. And a city built as one object cannot easily grow, shrink or be repaired the way a normal city does because a normal city is millions of separate small decisions made over centuries. There is a more basic problem too. Cities are not usually designed and then filled. They accumulate. Excavation and foundation work has genuinely happened. Satellite imagery shows a long construction corridor cut across the desert with significant earthworks. This is not purely a rendering. [music] Reporting has also indicated that the near-term scope has been reconsidered with far shorter initial sections [music] and much lower population targets discussed than the original announcement suggested. There has been sustained international reporting on [music] labor conditions and on communities displaced by the wider neon development [music] and that reporting is a serious part of the record. Now some of you are going to say this does not belong on a list of mega projects at all because a mega project should be something that exists. I take the point but I would argue the reverse. Everything else here got built and then reality argued with it afterward. This one is having the argument first in public at full scale with the earth already moved. Tell me below whether an unfinished idea counts. I do not think there is a clean answer. From a city that may never fill to a river that was built where no river [music] exists. Number six, the river that runs underneath a desert. Underneath the Sahara lies one of the largest reserves of fresh water on the planet. The Nubian sandstone aquafer system holds an enormous volume of groundwater beneath Libya, Egypt, Sudan, and Chad. It is fossil water. It fell as rain during periods when North Africa was far wetter than it is now, tens of thousands of years ago, and it has been sitting in the rock ever since. On any human time scale, it is not being replaced. Starting in the 1980s, Libya began building a system to bring that water north to [music] the coast where almost the entire population lives. The Great Man-made River is a network of enormous pipelines, thousands of kilometers of them, running from wellfields deep in the desert to the cities on the Mediterranean. The pipe sections are pre-stressed concrete [music] and large enough to drive a vehicle through. They were manufactured at plants built specifically for the purpose and hauled into the desert on specialized transporters. It is one of the largest water engineering projects ever attempted. And it delivers a very large volume of water every day to cities that would otherwise be in serious trouble. And it has one problem that no amount of engineering solves. The water does not [music] come back. Estimates of how long the aquifer can sustain extraction vary enormously depending on assumptions about volume, distribution, and how much can actually be pumped. Figures ranging from decades to many centuries have been published. And the honest position is that nobody can give you a confident number. Meanwhile, the system has to be maintained across thousands of kilometers of desert. During the conflict in Libya, infrastructure and the plants that made replacement pipe were damaged and maintenance became far harder in an unstable country. So, an entire population depends on water pumped from rock that filled up when the Sahara was green, moving through pipes that need constant repair in quantities nobody can precisely account for [music] on a clock nobody can precisely read. That project is spending water from the past. Our next one went looking for the past directly [music] and stopped when the rock stopped making sense. Number five, the hole that had to be abandoned. On the Cola Peninsula in northwestern Russia near the Norwegian border, there is a rusted metal cap bolted to a concrete pad. It looks like nothing. It is about 23 cm across. Underneath it is the deepest artificial hole ever drilled into the Earth. The Cola super deep bore hole was a Soviet scientific project begun in 1970. The goal was not oil. It was pure research to drill as deep into the continental crust as technology allowed and find out what was actually down there. Drilling continued for decades. The deepest branch reached over 12,200 m, more than 12 km straight down. It remains the deepest point humans have ever reached below the surface. [music] and what came back up rewrote assumptions. Seismic data had suggested that at a certain depth [music] the rock changed character and the expectation was a transition from granite to basalt. The drill got there and found no such boundary. The change in the seismic signal appeared instead to come from the granite itself being altered under intense pressure and temperature, fractured and saturated in a way nobody had accounted for. There was water down there in the rock [music] at depths where scientists had not expected free water to exist. Not water that had seeped down from the surface. Water that appeared to have been forced out of the minerals themselves and trapped by impermeable rock above. And in core samples from several kilome down, researchers reported microscopic [music] fossils, remnants of tiny marine organisms preserved in rock far below the surface. Then the project hit a wall that was not political. At those depths, the temperature climbed far higher than the models predicted. Rather than the expected figure, the rock at the bottom was reported to be around 180° C. At that temperature, the rock behaved differently. It became more plastic, less like brittle stone, and more like something that could flow slowly. The hole did not stay a clean hole. Drilling became extraordinarily difficult [music] and progress effectively halted. Work wound down through the 1990s and the site was shut down in the 2000s. The hole was sealed. 12 km into a planet with a radius of over 6,000. Two decades of work to [music] scratch the surface and the surface got hot enough and strange enough to stop them. That lid is still sitting up there in the tundra, welded shut over the deepest place we [music] have ever managed to reach. From a hole that was closed to a sea that was drained by accident. Number four, the mega project you can see from space by what is missing. The Aerrol Sea on the border of what is now Kazakhstan and Usbekiststan was once among the largest lakes on Earth. It supported a substantial fishing industry. There were ports and there were fleets. Beginning in earnest in the 1960s, Soviet planners undertook an enormous irrigation program to turn central Asian desert into cotton growing land. The two rivers feeding the Aerrol Sea, the Amuaria and the Seir Daria were diverted into a vast network of canals. The engineering achieved its stated goal. Cotton production rose enormously. The [music] consequence was understood in advance. Accounts indicate planners knew the sea would shrink. The calculation made was that the agricultural output was worth more than the lake. What appears not to have been fully grasped was how completely it would go and what would be left behind. The Arrol Sea lost the overwhelming majority of its volume. It broke into separate bodies of water. Fishing towns found themselves stranded tens of kilometers from any water at all. The ships did not move. There are widely photographed images of rusting fishing vessels sitting upright on dry sand surrounded by scrub [music] with camels walking past them. The exposed seabed was not clean. It was loaded with salt and with agricultural chemicals that had washed down the rivers for decades. Wind picks that dust up and carries it across the region. [music] And researchers have linked it to serious public health problems in surrounding communities. The local climate shifted with hotter summers and colder winters once the moderating effect of a huge body of water disappeared. There has been genuine recovery in one part. Kazakhstan built the Kokarall Dam completed in the mid 2000s to hold water in the northern section. The North Arol Sea has risen. Salinity has fallen and fish returned in numbers that supported a revived fishery. That is a real success and it deserves saying clearly. The larger southern portion has not recovered on anything like that scale. Every other project on this list is something humans built. This one [music] is a hole in the map the size of a sea produced by a system of canals working exactly as designed. From something that was lost to something that had to be sealed away in a hurry. Number three, the arch built to cover a disaster. After the reactor explosion at Chernobyl in 1986, a concrete and steel structure was built around the destroyed unit in extraordinary conditions. It was assembled at enormous speed by workers operating under severe radiation limits using remote techniques where possible and [music] human beings were not. That original sarcophagus was never meant to be permanent. It degraded over the following decades and there were serious concerns about its structural condition and about the possibility of a collapse releasing contaminated dust. So, a second structure was built, the new safe confinement. It is an enormous steel arch spanning more than 250 m and standing over 100 m tall, large enough to enclose the entire old sarcophagus and the ruined reactor building underneath it. And here is what makes it remarkable. as engineering. It could not be built where it was needed because radiation levels at the reactor made prolonged work there unacceptable. So, it was assembled some distance away in sections. And then in [music] 2016, the completed arch weighing over 30,000 tons was slid horizontally into position over the reactor on a rail and jacking system. One of the largest movable land-based structures ever built, pushed into place over the site of the worst nuclear accident in history, it was designed with a service life of a century, intended to allow the eventual dismantling of the ruins underneath in a controlled way using remote handling equipment installed inside. 100 years is a long time for a building. It is nothing at all for the material inside. In 2025, during the war in Ukraine, the confinement structure was reported to have been damaged by a drone strike that caused a fire and breached the outer cladding. [music] And international monitoring bodies reported concerns about its ceiling function, which is the thing nobody could design around. [music] Engineers can build a structure to survive a century of weather and radiation. They cannot build one that guarantees a century of peace around it. And that leads directly to the last two. Both of them attempts to solve a problem [music] that stretches far beyond any of us. Number two, the site built to be poisoned. At Hanford in Washington State, an enormous industrial complex was built starting in 1943 [music] as part of the Manhattan project. It produced plutonium, including material used in the first tested nuclear device and in the weapon dropped on Nagasaki, and it kept producing through the Cold War. What it also produced was waste. An enormous volume of highlevel radioactive liquid stored in underground tanks. Many of those tanks were single shell built decades ago and a number of them have leaked. Contamination has entered soil and groundwater in an area near the Colombia River. The cleanup has been running for decades and is projected to run for decades more. It is routinely described as one of the largest and most complex environmental remediation efforts in the world [music] with costs running into many tens of billions of dollars. Part of the solution is a treatment plant designed to lock waste into glass, a process called vitrification, melting the material into solid blocks far more stable than liquid in a steel [music] tank. That plant has been an enormous project in itself with a long history of redesigns, delays, and cost increases. The work at Hanford began during a world war that ended 80 years ago. The people who started it are gone. The cleanup will outlast everyone currently working on it and quite possibly everyone currently alive. It is a mega project whose entire purpose is to undo a previous mega project. And it is not close to finished. Which brings us to number one. Because one project has taken this problem to its logical conclusion and run into a question that engineering cannot answer. Number one, the tomb for a 100,000 years. On the island of Okiluto in Finland, a tunnel spirals down into ancient bedrock descending to a depth of roughly 430 m. It is called Enkalo, which in [music] Finnish means something close to cavity or hollow. It is being built as a permanent repository for spent nuclear fuel and it is the furthest advanced project of its kind in the world. The concept is deep geological disposal. Spent fuel is sealed inside copper canisters. Those canisters go into holes bored in the tunnel floor packed around with bentonite clay which swells when it meets water and [music] forms a barrier. The tunnels are backfilled and eventually the entire facility is sealed and the access route closed. The site was chosen for its geology. Very old, very stable crystallin rock studied for decades specifically to understand how it behaves and how water moves through it. The design time scale is what stops people in their tracks. The material has to remain isolated for something on the order of 100,000 years. Try to hold that number properly for a second. A 100,000 years ago, [music] our species had not spread across most of the planet. Every language spoken today is vastly younger than that. Every religion, every country, every alphabet, written history is a rounding error against it. Within that span, ice sheets have advanced across northern Europe and retreated again more than once. The engineers working on Enkalo have to account for future glaciation, for the weight of kilometers of ice pressing down, for the land rebounding upward afterward, for how groundwater chemistry might change over periods [music] that make all recorded human history look like an afternoon. And then there is the problem with no engineering solution at all. How do you warn people? This question has been taken entirely seriously and researchers have worked on it for decades in several countries. The difficulty is that every method of communication we have [music] ever invented degrades. Languages die. Symbols reverse their meaning. A skull and crossbones has meant poison [music] and piracy and a print on a child's shirt. Written warnings assume someone can read the language. Pictures assume shared visual conventions. And there is a deeper trap. A large, deliberately constructed, clearly important marked site is exactly the kind of thing human beings have always dug into. Every warning we have ever left on a sealed chamber has read to later generations as an advertisement that something valuable is inside. Proposals have included hostile landscapes of concrete spikes, enormous fields of menacing earthworks, and information stored in redundant layers. Others argue the opposite, that the safest approach is to seal it, restore the surface, tell nobody, and let the location be forgotten completely. Finland's approach has leaned toward that second philosophy. Once the repository is full and sealed, the intention is that it does not need to be maintained, monitored, or guarded. It is designed to be safe if it is simply left alone. Which means the plan in the end depends on forgetting. Every other project on this list was built to be used. Roads to drive on, [music] tunnels to travel through, dams to generate power, cities to live in. Their success is measured in how well they serve the people who are here. Ankalo is the only one designed to succeed by being abandoned. Its builders are quietly hoping that in a thousand generations, nobody remembers it exists. Nobody comes looking and the safest possible outcome is that their greatest work is never found at all. That is the thread running through all 15 of these. [music] We are extraordinarily good at building. We are much worse at predicting the consequences and worst of all at imagining the world that will be standing over our work long [music] after we are gone. Concai keeps sinking and engineers keep lifting it. The Gothur Mountain keeps pressing in and the linings keep giving way just enough. The aerrol seabed keeps [music] blowing across central Asia and under a finished forest a hole is being drilled with the specific intention that nobody ever should find it. If you made it all the way to the end, tell me in the comments which of these you think will still be standing in a thousand years and which one will be the first to fail. And you pick where we go next. Sunken cities swallowed whole by the sea or the deepest caves on Earth that nobody has ever reached the bottom of. Say the word below and I will make it. Subscribe and I will see you in the next thing humans built without quite knowing what would happen.

From the outside, it now looks like a finished building. There have been partial openings announced, lighting displays projected across the facade, and periodic reports that a section might open. The interior, by essentially every account that has come out, remains largely unfinished, which produces something genuinely strange. The tallest unoccupied building on the planet in the middle of a capital city, lit up at night, looking complete from every angle a photograph can be taken from. Nobody outside the country can tell you with confidence what is actually inside it. That is a building nobody can get into. Our next project is one that will not stay where its builders put it. [music] Number 14, the airport that will not stop sinking. By the late 1980s, Osaka in Japan had a serious problem. It needed a new international airport and there was no land available. The region is densely built and the old airport was hemmed in by a city that did not want to be woken up at night. So the solution was to build the land. Concai International Airport sits on an artificial island in Osaka Bay around 5 km offshore. Construction began in 1987. Crews leveled hilltops on the mainland and moved an enormous volume of fill out into the bay. They drove hundreds of thousands of vertical sand drains into the seabed to squeeze water out of the soft clay beneath, trying to force decades of natural settlement to happen in advance. The people doing [music] this were not amateurs. They knew the island would sink. That was expected. That was in the plan. It sank faster than the plan. By the time the airport opened in 1994, [music] the island had already settled substantially more than the projections allowed for. Buildings were fitted with adjustable columns, jacks, that let engineers lift sections of the terminal as [music] the ground beneath dropped unevenly. That system is still in use. The airport is in a real sense being manually held up. The settlement has slowed enormously as everyone [music] expected it would. But it has not stopped. And here is what makes it genuinely [music] difficult. The clay layers under Osaka Bay are not uniform. They compress at different rates in different places. And the deeper layers behave in ways that are hard to model precisely. Predictions of how much further it will settle have been repeatedly revised as the real measurements come in. In 2018, a typhoon pushed a storm surge over the island and flooded the runway and terminal, stranding thousands of people. Seaw walls have been raised since. So there it is. One of the busiest airports in Asia on ground that did not exist 40 years ago. Sitting on soft clay in a typhoon zone kept level by hand indefinitely. From an island that keeps dropping to a tunnel that took two centuries of arguing before anyone dug it properly. Number 13. The tunnel under the sea that took 200 years to start. The idea of a tunnel under the English Channel is not modern. A French engineer proposed one seriously in 1802, [music] complete with ventilation chimneys rising out of the water and a halfway island where horses could be changed. Napoleon reportedly showed interest. It went nowhere. Attempts kept coming through the 19th century. In the 1880s, exploratory tunnels were actually dug from both coasts. Real machinery, real [music] progress over a kilometer driven under the seabed. Then British military anxiety killed it. The argument was simple. A tunnel is a hole in a moat. And Britain's entire defensive logic rested on being an island. Work stopped. Another attempt in the 1970s was cancelled after digging had already begun. The tunnel that finally worked started in 1988 and opened in 1994. Three bores [music] around 50 km with roughly 38 km of that under the seabed. One of the longest undersea tunnel sections in the world. Geology made it possible. A layer of chalk marl runs under the channel relatively soft and relatively watertight and the tunnel follows it. Machines worked from both coasts and the breakthrough came in 1990. The engineering worked, the arithmetic did not. The project ran dramatically over budget and the private consortium financing it went through severe restructuring. shareholders lost enormous sums. It became a textbook case in how badly large infrastructure projects misjudge cost and revenue. Studied by economists ever since, precisely because so many smart people got the numbers so wrong. 200 years of proposals, a tunnel that works beautifully, [music] carries millions of people, and costs so much more than anyone forecast that the people who paid for it never got their money back. That project misjudged money. Our next one changed something considerably larger. Number 12, the dam that moved the day. On the Yangze River in China stands the Three Gorges Dam, the largest power station on the planet by [music] installed capacity. The wall is over 2 km wide and around 180 m high with a reservoir stretching hundreds of kilome upstream. The human cost was written into the plan from the start. Well over a million people were relocated. Entire cities were demolished and rebuilt on higher ground. Temples, towns, and archaeological sites that had stood for centuries went under the water permanently. The project was debated inside China for decades. It was approved by the National People's Congress in 1992 with an unusually large number of abstensions and votes against which in that body is a signal. Then there is the detail that circulates endlessly online. And unusually for these things, there is real science behind it. The reservoir holds an enormous mass of water, and filling it raised that mass higher above sea level than it had been. Moving mass away from the axis of a spinning object changes how it spins. NASA scientists calculated the effect, and the figure that came out was an increase in the length of the day of a fraction of a microscond. a tiny number, also a real one. Human beings built something big enough that the planet's rotation had to be recalculated. The harder questions are still being argued. Reservoir induced seismicity is a genuine field of study, and researchers have looked closely at whether the enormous water load and changing pressure in the rock have influenced seismic activity in the region. Landslides along the reservoir banks have been an ongoing documented problem as levels rise and fall. Sediment that used to travel down the Yangze now settles behind the dam instead with consequences downstream [music] that are still being measured. It generates a staggering amount of clean electricity. It also rearranged a river system that had behaved a certain way for millions of years and that accounting is not finished. That project delivered what it [music] promised at a cost people still argue over. Our next one delivered nothing at all for 9 years. Number 11, the airport that could not be switched on. Berlin decided in the 1990s to consolidate its airports into one modern hub. Construction on Berlin Brandenburgg airport began in 2006. The opening was [music] set for 2011. It opened in 2020. The delay became a national embarrassment. Opening dates were announced and cancelled repeatedly, sometimes within weeks of the date. Invitations went out. Airlines rescheduled operations. Then it was called off again. The core problem was the fire safety system. The smoke extraction design was extraordinarily [music] complex. And when inspectors examined it, it failed, not in a small way. Investigations reportedly identified tens of thousands of defects across the building with cable routing, [music] sprinkler installation, and the fire alarm system all implicated. [music] For years, staff ran lights and systems in the empty terminal simply to stop the equipment degrading, and trains ran through the unused station beneath it to keep the tunnel ventilated. Costs multiplied several times over the original budget. Executives resigned. Parliamentary committees investigated and the airport sat there finished on the outside completely unusable. Now I can hear the objection already. A delayed airport is a management failure, not a mystery. Nobody in Berlin is standing there unable to explain the physics. Fair enough. But Germany has one of the most respected engineering cultures on Earth. This project had money, expertise, oversight, [music] and enormous public attention. And a group of extremely competent people still could not get a building to pass its own fire [music] inspection for the better part of a decade. If that can happen there, the question is not why Berlin failed. [music] It is why we assume anywhere else would do better. Tell me in the comments whether you think this one earns its place. I suspect this is where we split from a project that could not open to a project that is quietly coming apart in the sea. Number 10, the islands that are going backwards. Off the coast of Dubai, the Palm Jira is one of the most recognizable shapes on Earth from the air. A palm tree made of sand with a trunk, 16 fronds, and a curving breakwater around the outside. It was dredged out of the seabed. Enormous volumes of sand were pumped into position and the breakwater [music] built from millions of tons of rock. To compact the fill and reduce the risk of it liquefying in a seismic event, contractors used viro compaction, driving probes into the sand and [music] shaking it into a denser state. It worked. People live there. Its bigger sibling did not fare as well. Nearby, a second project [music] called the world was built. Around 300 artificial islands arranged into a rough map of the continents sold to buyers who wanted their own country in miniature. Then the financial crisis arrived in 2008. Development largely [music] stalled and the sea kept working. Reports emerged that the islands were eroding, that sand was migrating, that channels between them were silting up, and the shapes [music] were losing definition. Those reports were disputed by the developer, and there has been ongoing development on some islands since. But for years, satellite images of the world showed a map of the continents slowly going soft at the edges. And there is a wider problem. Artificial islands change how water moves. Currents that ran along a coastline get interrupted. Sediment accumulates where it is not wanted, and beaches elsewhere lose the sand supply they depended on. Coastal engineers have raised concerns about circulation and water quality behind structures like these [music] because water that does not move well does not stay clean. You can build a map of the world out of sand and make it hold together with rock and money. What you cannot do is tell the ocean to stop rearranging it. From islands the sea keeps editing to a project that went underground and could not find the bottom of its own budget. Number nine, the most expensive road in American history. Boston had an elevated highway running straight through the middle of it. Opened in the 1950s, it carried far more traffic than it was designed for. It was permanently congested, [music] and it cut the city off from its own waterfront with a wall of concrete and steel. The solution was simple to describe and appalling to execute. Take the highway down, put it underground, do it without stopping traffic. The project, officially called the central artery and tunnel [music] project and universally called the Big Dig, ran from 1991 to 2007. [music] Crews had to tunnel underneath a city that was already there, threading around subway lines, utilities, and building foundations while keeping the elevated highway open above their heads. In one section, engineers used ground freezing, driving pipes into the earth and circulating coolant to turn saturated soil into a solid block. so tunneling could proceed beneath active railway lines. It worked. The highway came down, the tunnels went in, and the city got its waterfront back. The cost is what everybody remembers. [music] Original estimates were a fraction of the final figure. With financing included, the total ran well past $14 billion, the most expensive highway project in American history. Then in 2006, ceiling panels in one of the tunnels collapsed onto a car, killing a passenger. The investigation focused on the epoxy anchor system holding the panels, and the resulting inquiry dominated coverage of the project for years. A genuine engineering achievement that people drive through every day without thinking about it, tied permanently to a cost overrun taught in business schools, and to a death that should not have happened. Now, before we get to the top eight, do me one small favor. Hit the like button. It genuinely tells the algorithm to push this to more people who love this kind of thing, and it costs you nothing because the next ones stop being about money and start being about physics that does not cooperate. Number eight, the tunnel where the mountain closes in. Under the Swiss Alps runs the Godard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016. At around 57 kilometers, it is the longest railway tunnel in the world. And at its deepest, it lies roughly 2,300 meters below the mountains above. Building it took 17 years. Two enormous boring machines, plus sections excavated by blasting where the machines could not cope. The reason it took 17 years is that the Alps are not one thing. Boring through a mountain range means passing through a sequence of completely different rock types [music] and each one has its own opinion about being drilled. Some of it was hard, stable granite, which is comparatively good news, [music] and some of it was not. There are zones in these mountains where the rock behaves almost like something thick and slow rather than something solid. Under enormous pressure, certain rock types deform over time. Engineers call it squeezing ground. Once you cut a hole through it, the rock does not sit there. It creeps inward, closing the space you just made, pressing against whatever you installed to hold it open. Tunnel builders in the Alps have dealt with this for well over a century. And [music] the historic Godhard tunnel of the 1870s met exactly this problem. The techniques that work involve giving the rock somewhere to go rather than trying to stop it dead. Yielding supports, deformable elements that compress in a controlled way. linings designed on the assumption that the mountain will push and must be allowed to. Predicting exactly where those zones appear and how badly they behave is extremely difficult even with extensive survey work because you cannot see through 2 km of rock. Crews find out when they get there. Meanwhile, at that depth, rock temperatures climb high enough that the working environment has to be actively cooled for people to function. So, there is a train running under the Alps right now at high speed through a tunnel that took nearly two decades in a mountain that is still very slowly trying to close it. That project fought a mountain that was already there. Our next one proposes to build a mountain of its own. Number seven, the line in the desert. In 2021, Saudi Arabia announced [music] a project called the line, part of the wider neon development. The concept as presented was a city built as a single continuous structure. Two parallel mirrored walls around 500 m tall, stretching 170 km across the desert, roughly 200 m apart. No cars, everything you need within a 5-minute walk. Millions of residents. The renderings were spectacular and went everywhere. Engineers and urban planners raised questions immediately, and they were not unreasonable ones. A linear city means the two ends are 170 km apart, and the proposal relied on high-speed rail beneath it. Mirrored glass at that scale raises serious questions about bird strikes and about heat. A single continuous structure has to be built through varied terrain. And a city built as one object cannot easily grow, shrink or be repaired the way a normal city does because a normal city is millions of separate small decisions made over centuries. There is a more basic problem too. Cities are not usually designed and then filled. They accumulate. Excavation and foundation work has genuinely happened. Satellite imagery shows a long construction corridor cut across the desert with significant earthworks. This is not purely a rendering. [music] Reporting has also indicated that the near-term scope has been reconsidered with far shorter initial sections [music] and much lower population targets discussed than the original announcement suggested. There has been sustained international reporting on [music] labor conditions and on communities displaced by the wider neon development [music] and that reporting is a serious part of the record. Now some of you are going to say this does not belong on a list of mega projects at all because a mega project should be something that exists. I take the point but I would argue the reverse. Everything else here got built and then reality argued with it afterward. This one is having the argument first in public at full scale with the earth already moved. Tell me below whether an unfinished idea counts. I do not think there is a clean answer. From a city that may never fill to a river that was built where no river [music] exists. Number six, the river that runs underneath a desert. Underneath the Sahara lies one of the largest reserves of fresh water on the planet. The Nubian sandstone aquafer system holds an enormous volume of groundwater beneath Libya, Egypt, Sudan, and Chad. It is fossil water. It fell as rain during periods when North Africa was far wetter than it is now, tens of thousands of years ago, and it has been sitting in the rock ever since. On any human time scale, it is not being replaced. Starting in the 1980s, Libya began building a system to bring that water north to [music] the coast where almost the entire population lives. The Great Man-made River is a network of enormous pipelines, thousands of kilometers of them, running from wellfields deep in the desert to the cities on the Mediterranean. The pipe sections are pre-stressed concrete [music] and large enough to drive a vehicle through. They were manufactured at plants built specifically for the purpose and hauled into the desert on specialized transporters. It is one of the largest water engineering projects ever attempted. And it delivers a very large volume of water every day to cities that would otherwise be in serious trouble. And it has one problem that no amount of engineering solves. The water does not [music] come back. Estimates of how long the aquifer can sustain extraction vary enormously depending on assumptions about volume, distribution, and how much can actually be pumped. Figures ranging from decades to many centuries have been published. And the honest position is that nobody can give you a confident number. Meanwhile, the system has to be maintained across thousands of kilometers of desert. During the conflict in Libya, infrastructure and the plants that made replacement pipe were damaged and maintenance became far harder in an unstable country. So, an entire population depends on water pumped from rock that filled up when the Sahara was green, moving through pipes that need constant repair in quantities nobody can precisely account for [music] on a clock nobody can precisely read. That project is spending water from the past. Our next one went looking for the past directly [music] and stopped when the rock stopped making sense. Number five, the hole that had to be abandoned. On the Cola Peninsula in northwestern Russia near the Norwegian border, there is a rusted metal cap bolted to a concrete pad. It looks like nothing. It is about 23 cm across. Underneath it is the deepest artificial hole ever drilled into the Earth. The Cola super deep bore hole was a Soviet scientific project begun in 1970. The goal was not oil. It was pure research to drill as deep into the continental crust as technology allowed and find out what was actually down there. Drilling continued for decades. The deepest branch reached over 12,200 m, more than 12 km straight down. It remains the deepest point humans have ever reached below the surface. [music] and what came back up rewrote assumptions. Seismic data had suggested that at a certain depth [music] the rock changed character and the expectation was a transition from granite to basalt. The drill got there and found no such boundary. The change in the seismic signal appeared instead to come from the granite itself being altered under intense pressure and temperature, fractured and saturated in a way nobody had accounted for. There was water down there in the rock [music] at depths where scientists had not expected free water to exist. Not water that had seeped down from the surface. Water that appeared to have been forced out of the minerals themselves and trapped by impermeable rock above. And in core samples from several kilome down, researchers reported microscopic [music] fossils, remnants of tiny marine organisms preserved in rock far below the surface. Then the project hit a wall that was not political. At those depths, the temperature climbed far higher than the models predicted. Rather than the expected figure, the rock at the bottom was reported to be around 180° C. At that temperature, the rock behaved differently. It became more plastic, less like brittle stone, and more like something that could flow slowly. The hole did not stay a clean hole. Drilling became extraordinarily difficult [music] and progress effectively halted. Work wound down through the 1990s and the site was shut down in the 2000s. The hole was sealed. 12 km into a planet with a radius of over 6,000. Two decades of work to [music] scratch the surface and the surface got hot enough and strange enough to stop them. That lid is still sitting up there in the tundra, welded shut over the deepest place we [music] have ever managed to reach. From a hole that was closed to a sea that was drained by accident. Number four, the mega project you can see from space by what is missing. The Aerrol Sea on the border of what is now Kazakhstan and Usbekiststan was once among the largest lakes on Earth. It supported a substantial fishing industry. There were ports and there were fleets. Beginning in earnest in the 1960s, Soviet planners undertook an enormous irrigation program to turn central Asian desert into cotton growing land. The two rivers feeding the Aerrol Sea, the Amuaria and the Seir Daria were diverted into a vast network of canals. The engineering achieved its stated goal. Cotton production rose enormously. The [music] consequence was understood in advance. Accounts indicate planners knew the sea would shrink. The calculation made was that the agricultural output was worth more than the lake. What appears not to have been fully grasped was how completely it would go and what would be left behind. The Arrol Sea lost the overwhelming majority of its volume. It broke into separate bodies of water. Fishing towns found themselves stranded tens of kilometers from any water at all. The ships did not move. There are widely photographed images of rusting fishing vessels sitting upright on dry sand surrounded by scrub [music] with camels walking past them. The exposed seabed was not clean. It was loaded with salt and with agricultural chemicals that had washed down the rivers for decades. Wind picks that dust up and carries it across the region. [music] And researchers have linked it to serious public health problems in surrounding communities. The local climate shifted with hotter summers and colder winters once the moderating effect of a huge body of water disappeared. There has been genuine recovery in one part. Kazakhstan built the Kokarall Dam completed in the mid 2000s to hold water in the northern section. The North Arol Sea has risen. Salinity has fallen and fish returned in numbers that supported a revived fishery. That is a real success and it deserves saying clearly. The larger southern portion has not recovered on anything like that scale. Every other project on this list is something humans built. This one [music] is a hole in the map the size of a sea produced by a system of canals working exactly as designed. From something that was lost to something that had to be sealed away in a hurry. Number three, the arch built to cover a disaster. After the reactor explosion at Chernobyl in 1986, a concrete and steel structure was built around the destroyed unit in extraordinary conditions. It was assembled at enormous speed by workers operating under severe radiation limits using remote techniques where possible and [music] human beings were not. That original sarcophagus was never meant to be permanent. It degraded over the following decades and there were serious concerns about its structural condition and about the possibility of a collapse releasing contaminated dust. So, a second structure was built, the new safe confinement. It is an enormous steel arch spanning more than 250 m and standing over 100 m tall, large enough to enclose the entire old sarcophagus and the ruined reactor building underneath it. And here is what makes it remarkable. as engineering. It could not be built where it was needed because radiation levels at the reactor made prolonged work there unacceptable. So, it was assembled some distance away in sections. And then in [music] 2016, the completed arch weighing over 30,000 tons was slid horizontally into position over the reactor on a rail and jacking system. One of the largest movable land-based structures ever built, pushed into place over the site of the worst nuclear accident in history, it was designed with a service life of a century, intended to allow the eventual dismantling of the ruins underneath in a controlled way using remote handling equipment installed inside. 100 years is a long time for a building. It is nothing at all for the material inside. In 2025, during the war in Ukraine, the confinement structure was reported to have been damaged by a drone strike that caused a fire and breached the outer cladding. [music] And international monitoring bodies reported concerns about its ceiling function, which is the thing nobody could design around. [music] Engineers can build a structure to survive a century of weather and radiation. They cannot build one that guarantees a century of peace around it. And that leads directly to the last two. Both of them attempts to solve a problem [music] that stretches far beyond any of us. Number two, the site built to be poisoned. At Hanford in Washington State, an enormous industrial complex was built starting in 1943 [music] as part of the Manhattan project. It produced plutonium, including material used in the first tested nuclear device and in the weapon dropped on Nagasaki, and it kept producing through the Cold War. What it also produced was waste. An enormous volume of highlevel radioactive liquid stored in underground tanks. Many of those tanks were single shell built decades ago and a number of them have leaked. Contamination has entered soil and groundwater in an area near the Colombia River. The cleanup has been running for decades and is projected to run for decades more. It is routinely described as one of the largest and most complex environmental remediation efforts in the world [music] with costs running into many tens of billions of dollars. Part of the solution is a treatment plant designed to lock waste into glass, a process called vitrification, melting the material into solid blocks far more stable than liquid in a steel [music] tank. That plant has been an enormous project in itself with a long history of redesigns, delays, and cost increases. The work at Hanford began during a world war that ended 80 years ago. The people who started it are gone. The cleanup will outlast everyone currently working on it and quite possibly everyone currently alive. It is a mega project whose entire purpose is to undo a previous mega project. And it is not close to finished. Which brings us to number one. Because one project has taken this problem to its logical conclusion and run into a question that engineering cannot answer. Number one, the tomb for a 100,000 years. On the island of Okiluto in Finland, a tunnel spirals down into ancient bedrock descending to a depth of roughly 430 m. It is called Enkalo, which in [music] Finnish means something close to cavity or hollow. It is being built as a permanent repository for spent nuclear fuel and it is the furthest advanced project of its kind in the world. The concept is deep geological disposal. Spent fuel is sealed inside copper canisters. Those canisters go into holes bored in the tunnel floor packed around with bentonite clay which swells when it meets water and [music] forms a barrier. The tunnels are backfilled and eventually the entire facility is sealed and the access route closed. The site was chosen for its geology. Very old, very stable crystallin rock studied for decades specifically to understand how it behaves and how water moves through it. The design time scale is what stops people in their tracks. The material has to remain isolated for something on the order of 100,000 years. Try to hold that number properly for a second. A 100,000 years ago, [music] our species had not spread across most of the planet. Every language spoken today is vastly younger than that. Every religion, every country, every alphabet, written history is a rounding error against it. Within that span, ice sheets have advanced across northern Europe and retreated again more than once. The engineers working on Enkalo have to account for future glaciation, for the weight of kilometers of ice pressing down, for the land rebounding upward afterward, for how groundwater chemistry might change over periods [music] that make all recorded human history look like an afternoon. And then there is the problem with no engineering solution at all. How do you warn people? This question has been taken entirely seriously and researchers have worked on it for decades in several countries. The difficulty is that every method of communication we have [music] ever invented degrades. Languages die. Symbols reverse their meaning. A skull and crossbones has meant poison [music] and piracy and a print on a child's shirt. Written warnings assume someone can read the language. Pictures assume shared visual conventions. And there is a deeper trap. A large, deliberately constructed, clearly important marked site is exactly the kind of thing human beings have always dug into. Every warning we have ever left on a sealed chamber has read to later generations as an advertisement that something valuable is inside. Proposals have included hostile landscapes of concrete spikes, enormous fields of menacing earthworks, and information stored in redundant layers. Others argue the opposite, that the safest approach is to seal it, restore the surface, tell nobody, and let the location be forgotten completely. Finland's approach has leaned toward that second philosophy. Once the repository is full and sealed, the intention is that it does not need to be maintained, monitored, or guarded. It is designed to be safe if it is simply left alone. Which means the plan in the end depends on forgetting. Every other project on this list was built to be used. Roads to drive on, [music] tunnels to travel through, dams to generate power, cities to live in. Their success is measured in how well they serve the people who are here. Ankalo is the only one designed to succeed by being abandoned. Its builders are quietly hoping that in a thousand generations, nobody remembers it exists. Nobody comes looking and the safest possible outcome is that their greatest work is never found at all. That is the thread running through all 15 of these. [music] We are extraordinarily good at building. We are much worse at predicting the consequences and worst of all at imagining the world that will be standing over our work long [music] after we are gone. Concai keeps sinking and engineers keep lifting it. The Gothur Mountain keeps pressing in and the linings keep giving way just enough. The aerrol seabed keeps [music] blowing across central Asia and under a finished forest a hole is being drilled with the specific intention that nobody ever should find it. If you made it all the way to the end, tell me in the comments which of these you think will still be standing in a thousand years and which one will be the first to fail. And you pick where we go next. Sunken cities swallowed whole by the sea or the deepest caves on Earth that nobody has ever reached the bottom of. Say the word below and I will make it.
